prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction and experimental discovery of the quantum spin Hall effect and time-reversal-invariant topological insulators

statement.case_for: B050 is the discovery I can defend most readily against the prize criterion of a discovery or invention with identifiable originators. Kane and Mele introduced the Z2 classification and the quantum spin Hall state in a short, decisive pair of papers, and Molenkamp's group delivered the first experimental observation in HgTe/CdTe wells, with quantised edge conductance that is a direct, measurable signature. From my own experimental side, the edge and surface states have since been confirmed by independent transport and ARPES measurements across many material families, so the discovery is mature and not dependent on one laboratory. Six of eight members ranked it, four in their top three, which tells me it survives scrutiny from theorists, atomic physicists and an astroparticle experimentalist alike. In my opening I put the quantum cascade laser first because it is a concrete invention that I understand well from layered-semiconductor and interface work. In this round I note that no other member ranked B021 at all, so my first place there is a personal view that has not been tested by the committee, and I do not think it is right to hold it ahead of a candidate that has broad cross-field support and a cleaner attribution story.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservations are attribution and overlap. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe quantum-well realisation that Molenkamp's experiment tested, and the three-dimensional generalisations (Fu, Kane, Mele; Moore and Balents) are outside the credited names, so three names cannot represent the whole history, and a committee would have to defend leaving them out. The 2016 prize for topological phases and phase transitions also sits close in subject, so we must be able to say that the Z2 insulator and the quantum spin Hall effect are a distinct achievement and not a second helping of the same idea. There is further a fair question of whether a prize centred on the two-dimensional effect is the right framing when three-dimensional topological insulators arguably had the larger materials impact.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B050 first as a conceptually clean discovery whose symmetry-based classification now underpins how band structure is classified and computed, while noting that Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and Fu are left out and that the 2016 prize raises an overlap question.
responses.response: I agree on the substance and I share the attribution worry. Where I would add something is the experiment: the HgTe result matters because it is a quantised, measurable edge conductance and not only a classification, so I would keep Molenkamp in the configuration even though the BHZ proposal preceded it. I would also resist treating 2016 as covering this. Thouless, Haldane and Kosterlitz honoured topological phase transitions and quantum Hall-type topology, while Kane and Mele supplied a time-reversal-invariant state with no net magnetic field, which was not anticipated by that work. I would like the citation to say this explicitly so that the committee can defend the distinction.

responses.point: Pearce ranks B009 first on instrumentation grounds but also places B050 third, accepting the prediction-plus-discovery structure while flagging the BHZ omission and the 2016 overlap, and asking whether the experiment is a sufficient component or the prize should be theory-only.
responses.response: I disagree with a theory-only prize. Without the HgTe measurement the Kane-Mele prediction would have remained one of several candidate states, and the observation is what made it a discovery in the sense the prize criteria use. I accept that this gives Molenkamp a role that is real but depends on the earlier BHZ proposal, which is a genuine qualification and one I cannot resolve with the credited names provided. On B009, I fully respect the instrumentation case, but a one-name credit for a collaboration-scale result looks harder to defend than a three-name theory-plus-experiment configuration, and I would want the committee to be clear who else built the detector concept before putting it above B050.

responses.point: Lindroth puts the optical lattice clock first for its conceptual clarity and metrological reach, and regards B050 as important but outside her own specialty, ranking it fourth.
responses.response: I take the clock case seriously and I ranked B051 myself, though low. Katori and Ye are a natural pair and the maturity is excellent. My hesitation is that the committee has to argue its novelty against the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize, and the benefit to the redefinition of the second is still prospective. I would put B051 ahead of B002 on maturity grounds, but I do not see it as stronger than B050 on originality and breadth of influence. I would also ask whether your ranking of B050 reflects doubt about the science or only distance from the field, because it is a topic that experimentalists in materials physics see in the lab every day.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks inflation first as the strongest conceptual advance, while conceding that no primordial gravitational-wave signal is seen and that credit beyond Guth, Linde and Mukhanov, notably Starobinsky, makes the allocation untidy.
responses.response: I would not argue with the conceptual weight of inflation, but by his own account the mechanism is not uniquely confirmed and the credit is not clean, whereas for B050 the observations are direct and independently reproduced. The prize is for a discovery or invention with identifiable originators, and I think that criterion currently favours candidates where the measurement stands behind the idea. Nothing prevents inflation from becoming the stronger case later if the tensor signal or another discriminating test arrives.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can defend omitting Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, whose HgTe proposal preceded and enabled the Molenkamp experiment.
Whether the 2016 prize on topological phases is judged sufficiently distinct from the quantum spin Hall and Z2 topological insulator discovery.
Whether the central credit lies with the two-dimensional quantum spin Hall effect or with three-dimensional topological insulators, which the credited names do not cover.
Whether B021 (quantum cascade laser) deserves a second look given that the credit of Cho versus Kazarinov and Suris is unresolved and no other member ranked it.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for the preferred configuration or the alternatives. I am a Chalmers colleague of Göran Johansson, who ranks B038 first, but no credited name on the shortlist is documented as being at Chalmers or a close collaborator of mine. I have documented ties to David R. Clarke (IBM), who is not credited here, and to Japanese universities and the microscopy federation, which do not touch the credited names; Hidetoshi Katori (B051) is Japan-based and I would note this only as a general academic exchange connection, not a personal one.
